title: Kumarajiva
hookLine: the translator who put the Lotus, Diamond and Vimalakirti into Chinese that people still read
tomorrow: The tongue that did not burn

lines: A DREAM, A BUBBLE, DEW, LIGHTNING.
cards: All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, like lightning. That is the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra as it's chanted in Chinese in East Asian temples.
The Chinese they chant comes from a translation made in Chang'an, by a team gathered around one monk born in an oasis town on the Silk Road.
Quick pictures, each gone almost as soon as it appears, set down in a Chinese that still sounds clear. His name was Kumarajiva.

teach.b: First, where he came from. His biography says he was born in Kucha, one of those oasis towns, to a mother from the royal family and a father from India. He became a monk as a boy and studied in Kashmir.
He knew the texts, and he came to know Chinese. Second, the long wait.

teach.h: HELD FOR YEARS ON THE FRONTIER.
teach.b: When a Chinese army took Kucha, Kumarajiva was carried off by a general and held for years in a frontier town. There, some readers think, his Chinese grew strong. Third, the work.
A later ruler brought him to the capital, Chang'an, and gave him a large team of monks and scholars.
Kumarajiva would hold the text, speak it in Chinese and discuss the hard words with the team, and the scribes would write.
From that room came the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Vimalakirti Sutra in the versions still chanted and studied. Fourth, his way of translating.

His biography tells a story: he said that turning Sanskrit into Chinese is like chewing rice before feeding it to someone. The flavor is lost, and the food may even turn the stomach. He knew what translation costs.
Even so, his versions read as clear, flowing Chinese that people could actually say aloud, and some readers credit that clarity for how long they've lasted.
So the week closes: old texts read again, a southern road, monks with merchants, translators at a table, a white horse, and now the translator whose words people still say.

how: In Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese temples, Kumarajiva's versions of the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra are chanted in services and studied in classes.

o: the Chinese name for the Diamond Sutra
a monk from Kucha whose Chinese sutras are still read
an Indian king who first sent monks to China

p: the oasis town where he was born
a dream, a bubble, dew, lightning

s: Kumarajiva worked alone in a quiet cell
he worked with a large team in Chang'an, speaking the text in Chinese while scribes wrote.
his biography says he was held for years on the frontier
a general carried him off from Kucha and kept him there.
his versions read as stiff, word-for-word Chinese
they read as clear, flowing Chinese, even though he said translation loses the flavor.

games.q: you're Kumarajiva. a phrase in the Sanskrit is exact but would sound clumsy in Chinese. what do you do?
o: keep it word for word, however it sounds.
make it clear Chinese that people can read, even if some flavor is lost.
games.why: his versions read as clear, readable Chinese. his chewed-rice saying admits what is lost, and his versions are the ones people still chant.

practice: Say the six pictures from the hook aloud once, giving each its own pause: a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, lightning. Then let each out-breath be one of them, let it go, and start again.

wordCard.voice: Kumarajiva. The monk from Kucha whose Chinese translations of the Lotus, the Diamond and the Vimalakirti Sutras are still read and chanted.

orig.note: Sanskrit form of the translator's name, Kumārajīva.

carryVoice: Your line: the translator. Something is always lost, and still the words carry. That's the week.
